Where a place has few records, show actual dated records, not a noise histogram. Pure export + template change.

PHASE 2 (bloom ingest -- new iNat data): scope = all-angiosperm per place PLUS the full target-host set (incl. endemics). Two orientations from one dataset: place-centric ('what blooms here, when') + host-centric ('where/when is this target plant, per county'). Method = random sampling (order_by=random, confirmed supported by iNat ES backend) of a few hundred obs per taxon to get the bloom-timing SHAPE cheaply; exhaustive fetch fallback for low-volume rare taxa (sampling misses presence). Respect API limits (60 req/min, 200/page, 10k cap->id_above). Location = bbox query + local polygon filter in DuckDB; obscured coords tolerated. Output = static aggregate JSON (static-hosting preserved).

TWO SIGNALS / TWO CADENCES:
- Bloom CLIMATOLOGY (slow): monthly, DECOUPLED from nightly, heavy crawl. Grain = place x week + target-host x county x week. Answers 'when to plan a trip'.
- Bloom NOWCAST (fast): nightly, cheap, TARGET-HOSTS ONLY, growing-season-gated. Recent-window (d1 ~last 2 weeks) query -> 'blooming NOW' flag, optionally sharpened by Flowers/Fruits annotation (term_id=12) where present. The activation liveness hook ('X just started blooming in Klickitat Co, go this week'). Place pages show both climatology + live flag.

title: Publish a slim collector login -> page map for search links
description:
ADR 0028: a search row links to the thing's page when one exists, and the href is
always supplied, never derived. Taxa and places have that today; PEOPLE DO NOT, so
person rows currently carry href: null (beeatlas-7nx.5).

Why it cannot just be `/collectors/${login}/`: a collector page exists only for the
entries in collectors.json (_pages/collector-detail.njk paginates
collectors.collectorsArray). Measured 2026-08-03: 124 logins have pages, but 158
distinct host_inat_login values appear on occurrences — 34 of them (22%) would 404.

Why it cannot just fetch collectors.json: 2.8 MB, and not in the runtime manifest at
all. Far too heavy for the boot path to learn 124 strings.

The shape already exists for taxa — src/taxon-pages.ts + the `taxon_pages` manifest
key, emitted by the SITE build from the very lists Eleventy paginates over, so it
cannot disagree with the pages that build produced. Do the same for collectors:
emit a login -> href map in scripts/postbuild-data.mjs, add a manifest key, load it
lazily like loadTaxonPages, and feed it to the `people` sources in
_rebuildSearchIndex.

Same rule as taxa: absent from the map means no link. A dead link is worse than a
plain-text name.
close_reason: Closed

title: County was fabricated for out-of-state records by an uncapped nearest-county fallback
description:
FIXED in f78e0218. Root cause was not bad coordinates — the coordinates are fine.

NO DATASET ASSERTS THE COUNTY. It is derived in marts/occurrences by
point-in-polygon, with a nearest-neighbour fallback that had NO DISTANCE CEILING.
For a point outside every Washington county the fallback returned the nearest one
regardless of distance, so "not in Washington" became a specific, plausible county
name indistinguishable downstream from a real assignment.

The exemplar, WSDA_2336960 / ecdysis:5597391:
  Ecdysis source row   county=Baker, state_province=Oregon, locality=near Snake River
  iNat 178085788       44.4880, -117.2202, accuracy 7 m, not obscured
  BeeAtlas published   Asotin County — 168 km away, beating Garfield by 2 km

The Ecdysis `county` and `state_province` columns exist in ecdysis_data.occurrences
and are dropped in staging; they never reach the mart.

THE FIX. A ceiling of 0.2 degrees on both the county and ecoregion fallbacks
(macros/region_snap_tolerance.sql). Measured over the corpus, points outside every
county split cleanly with an empty band between them:

  <= 0.140   20 points   Puget Sound, the Strait, the San Juans, the Columbia at
                         Cowlitz/Wahkiakum, the Idaho line at Whitman — all
                         Washington-adjacent, all snapping to the right county
  >= 0.278   16 points   Portland, Mount Hood, the Idaho panhandle, BC, the Oregon
                         bank of the Snake, and one in Arizona

0.2 sits in the gap, so it is a threshold rather than a tuning knob: 0.15 to 0.27
all classify identically. Beyond it county is NULL — the record is kept, because an
out-of-state specimen is real data and NULL is the true answer about which
Washington county it is in.

state_province was considered as the mechanism and rejected: 12 of the 16 have no
Ecdysis row (they are iNat records), so it would have fixed a quarter of them. It
remains the better cross-check where it exists.

Ecoregion keeps its value for 13 of the 16, correctly — stg_geo__ecoregions is
UNCLIPPED, so an Idaho panhandle point is genuinely inside the Columbia
Mountains/Northern Rockies polygon. Only 3 lose one.

GUARD: tests/assert_county_snap_within_tolerance.sql asserts the invariant directly
rather than trusting the fallback to keep its ceiling. Verified it fires on the old
mart (16 rows) and passes on the new one. Built occurrences+ downstream: 22 pass,
0 errors.

CORRECTION to an earlier comment in this thread: I said the BC record reading
San Juan in one build and Whatcom in another was explained by the county-geometry
simplification interacting with ST_Distance. That was wrong — the spatial join uses
stg_geo__us_counties at full resolution and was never touched by beeatlas-0yv. The
two readings come from different data vintages; with the ceiling in place that
record is NULL in both, so the instability is moot.

REMAINING, deliberately not done here: nothing tells a curator these 16 records
have out-of-state coordinates. They are now honestly county-less rather than
misfiled, but finding them still takes a query. A surfaced flag, or simply feeding
Ecdysis's own state_province through staging as a cross-check, would close that.
close_reason: Fixed in f78e0218: 0.2-degree ceiling on the county and ecoregion nearest-neighbour fallbacks, chosen from a clean empty band in the measured distribution, plus a dbt test asserting the invariant. 16 fabricated counties become NULL; the 20 legitimate offshore/border snaps are unchanged. Ships on the next nightly.

title: Basemap bleeds past Washington at low zoom, then retreats quadrant by quadrant
description:
Reported while running the beeatlas-ecn sweep. Zoomed out to ~z1.3 the map draws
North America and Greenland; zooming in, those areas blank to grey BEFORE they
leave the viewport, and most of the frame outside WA is grey. Hillshade never
appears outside WA at any zoom.

NOT A DEFECT — it is what a whole-tile extract looks like. data/build-basemap.sh
runs 'pmtiles extract --region=data/basemap/wa.geojson'. That keeps every tile
that INTERSECTS the polygon, and it keeps them whole: tile contents are never
clipped. At low zoom one tile is a continent, so the tile containing Washington
also contains everything else in its quadrant, free.

Measured against the live archive by probing the 'earth' layer:

  z1.3   WA, Kansas, Greenland, Montreal all land   (tile z1/0/0 = lng -180..0, lat 0..85)
  z2.5   WA, Kansas land; Greenland, Montreal grey  (tile z2/0/1 = lng -180..-90, lat 0..66.5)
  z4     WA land; Kansas grey

Each step halves the tile, so the bonus geography retreats toward WA. Exactly the
'disappears again as I zoom in, before leaving the viewport' behaviour.

The hillshade behaves differently because data/terrain_tiles.py rasterizes a DEM
that only covers the WA bbox — a raster genuinely has no data outside it, whereas
a vector tile carries whatever OSM put in it.

SO THE QUESTION IS COSMETIC: should out-of-region area read as deliberate rather
than broken? Options, cheapest first:

  1. Nothing. Grey is honest: there is no data there.
  2. A minZoom on the map (say 6) so the zoom levels where the bleed is most
     jarring are simply unreachable. Also stops people zooming to the whole globe
     for a Washington atlas.
  3. maxBounds around WA, which additionally stops panning to Idaho and finding
     nothing.
  4. A masking layer — a polygon of everything-except-WA drawn over the basemap
     in the background colour. Makes the edge crisp and intentional, costs a
     shipped geometry.

Prefer 2 or 3; they are one line each and also fix the 'why can I pan to Ohio'
version of the same question. Not urgent.
close_reason: minZoom 5 makes the pathological range unreachable — a URL asking for z1.3 clamps, scroll-out stops there, and a 393px phone still fits the state with margin. The residual edge on a wide desktop is left deliberately: masking it needs a shipped geometry or maxBounds, and maxBounds would fence off the out-of-state coordinate errors now tracked as beeatlas-8pz.

title: [bug] Location-denied message names Settings → Safari on every platform
description:
Found in the beeatlas-ecn map-interaction sweep, step D3.

Denying the geolocation permission shows a clear, dismissible banner and the app
stays fully interactive — that part is correct. The COPY is not:

  src/bee-atlas.ts:690
  'Location access is blocked. To enable, go to Settings → Safari → Location.'

That string is unconditional on _locationErrorKind === 'denied', so a desktop
Chrome or Firefox user, or an Android user, is told to open a Settings → Safari
path that does not exist on their device. Verified in headless Chromium: the
banner renders with the Safari wording.

The iOS PWA is the primary field surface, so the wording is right for the common
case and wrong for the rest. Options: branch on a coarse platform sniff, or fall
back to platform-neutral copy ('Location access is blocked. Re-enable it in your
browser or system settings.') with the Safari path added only when the UA is iOS
Safari.

Not urgent — nobody is blocked, the error is honest about WHAT happened, only
about how to fix it.
close_reason: iOS keeps its tested wording behind isIosSafari(); every other platform gets copy that is true rather than naming a Settings screen that does not exist. Both branches verified rendering in a browser.

title: Flaky: test_ecdysis_probe zip fixtures differ across a second boundary
description:
tests/test_ecdysis_probe.py::_fake_zip_bytes builds a ZIP with zipfile.ZipFile, which stamps each entry with the current DOS date/time. Tests that compare a response built by _zip_response() against a freshly-built _fake_zip_bytes('fresh') therefore fail whenever a one-second boundary falls between the two constructions.

Observed 2026-08-02 during beeatlas-8py: test_skip_probe_disabled_downloads_unconditionally failed with 'At index 10 diff: b"\xab" != b"\xac"' (index 10 is inside the local file header's mod-time field). Not reproducible by seed — it is wall-clock timing, not test order; 5 seeds x both trees all passed.

FIX: pin the timestamp, e.g. zf.writestr(zipfile.ZipInfo('occurrences.tab', date_time=(1980,1,1,0,0,0)), ...), so the bytes are a pure function of the marker. Affects every helper in that file that round-trips zip bytes through an equality assert.

title: Legacy collector JSON artifacts still in the docroot (16.5 MB + 2.9 MB)
description: The served /data holds collector_event_pages-<hash>.json (16.5 MB) and collectors-<hash>.json (2.9 MB), neither of which is in lib/runtime-artifacts.js — they predate the Model Y slim manifest. They are not fetched on the atlas cold load (beeatlas-tb8 measured that), so this is not a page-weight bug, but: does anything still read them? If the collector pages fetch them at runtime, they want the same pre-compression treatment as beeatlas-tb8 gave the atlas artifacts (collectors.json should gzip very well). If nothing reads them, they are 19 MB of docroot that merge-swap's 30-day prune will quietly remove and nobody will notice — which is the answer, but worth confirming rather than assuming.

title: Basemap: nothing renders outside Washington
description:
Fallout from beeatlas-q73, visible in UAT and deliberate but unfinished.

The WA PMTiles archive is clipped to the state, so everything beyond the border paints as the Protomaps theme's flat background — no coastline, no rivers, no place names. Mapbox served a global basemap, so this is a visible regression for anyone working near Portland, Coeur d'Alene, or the Canadian border, and the failure looks like a broken map rather than a bounded one.

Options, cheapest first:
 1. Nothing. The atlas is a WA project; document it and move on.
 2. A styled treatment for out-of-archive area — a distinct tint plus the state outline drawn from the counties GeoJSON already loaded, so the edge reads as "outside the survey area" rather than "tiles failed".
 3. Widen the archive. build-basemap.sh takes a bbox; a buffer of ~50 km costs tens of MB and is the only option that actually shows Portland. Interacts with the ~238 MB offline prime (beeatlas-6rs).

Related: the multi-state expansion intent (memory project_multi_state_expansion) makes the archive's extent a configuration question rather than a constant, whenever that lands.

title: Basemap: hillshade raster PMTiles, faded out above z13
description:
Optional, later, independently shippable. Build a z0-11 terrarium raster pyramid for WA (~20 MB measured) as a raster PMTiles, shipped through the same separate basemap path.

Style: raster-dem source (encoding: terrarium) + hillshade layer inserted BELOW the first symbol layer, faded out above ~z13 (interpolate hillshade-exaggeration to 0 by z13.5, or maxzoom). The fade is not cosmetic: measured, a z12 DEM overzoomed to z14 DARKENS the map and makes trails harder to read, and capping the display zoom is also what makes a cheap z11 DEM sufficient (it is native at the zooms where it shows). This is why the terrain budget is ~20 MB and not the 1459 MB a z13 pyramid would cost.

Offline: add to the prime list (+20 MB). Rollback is removing one layer and one source.

NOTE for the future 'regions above elevation X' idea: derive elevation-band polygons in the DATA PIPELINE (elevation_dem_m already exists per ADR 0015; the client already filters on it via ELEV_SQL, src/filter.ts:146) and ship them like counties/ecoregions. Client-side DEM queries would need full-precision high-zoom tiles — the 1.4 GB we rejected. So nothing here forecloses it.
acceptance_criteria: Rainier reads as terrain at z11-13; Paradise at z14 is no less legible than without hillshade; offline prime includes it.
notes:
RETUNED 2026-08-02 after on-device review (1af8e31b). The shipped values in the close reason above are superseded:

  fade ramp   12.5 -> 13.5   BECAME   13.0 -> 15.0
  layer maxzoom  (none)      BECAME   15.0 (= TERRAIN_FADE_END)

On a phone the original read as fading both too early and too abruptly — one zoom level is a fast change while pinching, and it removed the relief while landform was still what you were reading. Full strength now holds through z13 and the remainder spreads over two levels.

KNOWN TRADEOFF, deliberately accepted: z14 now carries ~23% exaggeration where it previously had none, and z14 is where trails first matter most. If trails ever read muddy at Paradise-like zooms, pulling TERRAIN_FADE_END back to ~14.5 is the fix, not lowering TERRAIN_EXAGGERATION (which would also weaken z11-13, where it is doing its job).

The layer maxzoom is a bandwidth fix, not a visual one: without it MapLibre kept range-requesting DEM tiles above the fade for a hillshade nobody could see. Measured over the tunnel — z13 = 3 terrain requests (header + 2 tiles), z16 = 1 (archive header only, unavoidable while the source is declared). Worth remembering for beeatlas-6rs: the header read happens regardless of zoom, so an offline reader still has to satisfy it.
close_reason:
Shipped f5473fa6 + b0e49376 + bdd10427. Terrain archive wa-terrain-20260802.pmtiles (60.8 MB) published on maderas 2026-08-02; hillshade live at regions.wa.terrain.

VERIFIED IN THE APP (local dev proxying /basemap/tiles to beeatlas.net):
- z11 Rainier reads as terrain; z13 at half-fade still legible with trails and peak labels crisp; z14 Paradise hillshade fully gone, trails unaffected. Both acceptance criteria met.
- Live style check: raster-dem/terrarium/tileSize 256, exaggeration ramp [12.5, 0.45] -> [13.5, 0], layer order earth(1) < landuse_park(3) < field_hillshade(14) < water(15) < water_stream(16) < roads_other(37) < firstSymbol(58).
- Serving: 206 + Content-Range, no Content-Encoding; pmtiles CLI reads the remote archive (tile type webp, 1913 tiles).

THREE DEVIATIONS FROM THIS ISSUE AS WRITTEN:
1. SIZE. '~20 MB measured' was a z0-10 figure. z0-11 raw is 200 MB. Two lossless transforms got it to 60.8 MB: round elevation to 1 m (200->92, worst case error 0.496 m, rounded not truncated) and lossless WebP instead of PNG (92->61, verified pixel-identical in MapLibre). z10 was built and compared side by side at 21.9 MB and rejected on looks -- ridges smear at z12. User chose z11 with the evidence.
2. LAYER POSITION. Not 'below the first symbol layer'. protomaps-themes-base interleaves fills and lines, so its first symbol layer is index 57; inserting there washes every road, trail and stream with shading in the one style that exists to make trails legible. Anchored under the 'water' fill instead: above earth/landcover/landuse_park, below water, streams, roads and all labels.
3. BUILD HOST. Not maderas. Unlike build-basemap.sh (a network extract), this is CPU-bound: ~11 tiles/min on maderas's 2 cores = ~3 h pinning the live web server, vs ~9 min on a laptop for a 61 MB upload. build-terrain-basemap.sh and the runbook now document build-locally-then-scp.

FOLLOW-UPS FILED/UPDATED: beeatlas-6rs gets the +61 MB prime member (and the note that terrain is the natural first thing to shed under storage pressure, since absent terrain already degrades gracefully); beeatlas-mas gets the four ADR-worthy decisions; beeatlas-r9t is an unrelated flaky test found en route.

NOT DONE, deliberately: offline priming (belongs to 6rs, which owns the Cache Storage byte store) and polygon clipping (~15%/9 MB for a point-in-polygon pass that must keep border-clipped tiles; declined).

title: Emit the group-map palette from the pipeline instead of computing it twice
description: Swatch colors are computed in data/species_maps.py AND re-implemented in _data/species.js (hslToHex, 'do NOT refactor — numerical equivalence is load-bearing'). ADR 0022 fixed the predicate drift and added an output parity test, but the duplication remains, including a known off-by-one at some hues (colorsys 127.49999999999991 vs JS 127.5). Publishing canonical_name -> hex from the pipeline (artifact + manifest key) would delete the second implementation. See ADR 0022 rejected alternatives.

title: Genus page hides community observations for specimen-less species
description: The species-list count line branches on occurrence_count > 0 (Ecdysis specimens) and otherwise falls through to the checklist branch, so Chelostoma phaceliae reads '2 checklist records' while the map draws 3 dots — its 1 community observation is not mentioned anywhere on the genus page. Consider branching on specimen_count > 0 OR inat_obs_count > 0 first. Related: ADR 0022 (the swatch half of the same confusion).

title: Search on the static pages: navigate to the app with a query
description:
beeatlas-v66 gated the header search button behind searchEnabled, which only <bee-atlas> sets — the species/places/collectors/taxon pages mount the same header through src/entries/bee-header.ts with no client-side store, so a button there could not answer.

Making search genuinely global means: a query URL param the app resolves on boot, a decision about what a species page does with a taxon hit, and the entry controller navigating to /index.html?q=… . See ADR 0021 'rejected alternatives'.

title: Restore the stale-install diagnostic: identify the RUNNING bundle, not the latest publish
description:
Spun out of beeatlas-4uj by review (Fable, 2026-07-31), which caught an overclaim in ADR 0019.

Moving the build id out of the bundle and into the slim manifest was right for the gate and right for beeatlas-96m's rule, but it is a TRADE, not a strict improvement, and the ADR originally said otherwise.

The two placements answer different questions:
  - BAKED INTO THE BUNDLE, the id travelled with the code, so it named WHAT YOU WERE RUNNING. A reused bundle kept naming whichever commit last rebuilt it — the flaw that motivated 4uj — but a stale installed PWA showed its own stale id.
  - FROM THE MANIFEST, over a NetworkFirst route, it names THE LATEST PUBLISH THE CLIENT CAN REACH. Correct for "what is deployed", wrong in the stale-install case: an old PWA, online, now displays today's sha while running last week's chunks.

The row's original stated purpose was the latter case — vite.config.ts's deleted comment read "so a stale installed PWA is diagnosable at a glance (iOS keeps an old SW + caches across reinstalls)". So the capability is gone, and the ADR now says so.

THE HONEST REPLACEMENT: the running chunk's own content hash. It ships with the code by construction, needs no `define`, and cannot go stale — because it IS the code. `import.meta.url` inside a bundled module resolves to that chunk's hashed URL (e.g. /assets/bee-header-B3MxoDCw.js), so the hash is readable at runtime with no build wiring at all. In dev it resolves to the source path, which is the natural 'dev' case.

Shape to consider: show both, and let them disagree visibly — "Build <publish-sha> · running <chunk-hash>" is ugly, but the DISAGREEMENT is the diagnostic. A stale install is precisely the case where the manifest's id and the running chunk's hash do not correspond, and detecting that automatically ("this install is out of date — reload") is more useful than either string alone. Note the app already has an update banner for the DATA; this would be its code-side twin.

Not urgent: the stale-install diagnostic was never load-bearing, and nothing regressed that anyone depends on today. Do it if PWA staleness bites again, or fold it into whatever next addresses the update banner.
acceptance_criteria: The menu can distinguish 'this install is running current code' from 'this install is stale', without any per-commit value inside a content-hashed chunk.

title: Nightly gate runs npm run build a second time inside test:data
description:
Found while diagnosing the 2026-07-31 aborted nightly (beeatlas-4oa deploy).

src/tests/build-output.data.test.ts runs execSync('npm run build') in beforeAll — it builds the site as its own fixture. The nightly then runs `npm run build` AGAIN as its site-build step. So every nightly performs two full site builds (~16s each on maderas), and the published output is the SECOND one while the gate's assertions were made against the FIRST.

Two things to weigh, and they pull in opposite directions:
  - Wasted work: one of the two builds is redundant, ~16s of a nightly with 24h of headroom. Low value on its own.
  - Soundness: the gate does not assert against the artifact that gets published. They are byte-identical in practice (same inputs, deterministic build), so this is theoretical today — but it is exactly the kind of gap that stops being theoretical the moment anything between the two builds is nondeterministic or the data dir moves under them.

Options: have the gate assert against the already-built _site and let the nightly build first (VITEST_SKIP_BUILD=1 already exists as the escape hatch); or keep the fixture build and drop the nightly's separate one. The second is likelier correct — the gate would then be gating the very tree it publishes.

Also note the ordering interaction with the beeatlas-4oa build receipt: whichever build runs LAST writes it, and the receipt describes _site, so today it is the nightly's own build that the receipt attests to. That is correct as it stands; a fix here must keep it so.
acceptance_criteria: A nightly performs one site build, and the gate's assertions are made against the tree that gets published.
close_reason: Fixed. The nightly built the site twice — build-output.data.test.ts builds it in a beforeAll, then the nightly built again — so it asserted against one tree and published another. Now it builds once, first, and BEEATLAS_SITE_PREBUILT=1 points the gate at that tree. VITEST_SKIP_BUILD was deliberately NOT reused (it skips the whole suite, so it would have disabled the gate rather than redirected it), and the alternative of letting the test's beforeAll be the only build was rejected: the published artifact must not be a test framework's side effect. The flag verifies its own precondition and vitest still exits 1 on a beforeAll throw (checked — the summary says 'skipped', so the exit code is what makes it a gate). Gate 11.0s -> 4.4s and a whole ~17s build dropped. Deployed; the nightly's own numbering fixed too (it had skipped step 5).

title: [bug] vite-plugin-preload has never run in production
description:
Found while doing beeatlas-d3y. The built site contains ZERO rel=preload tags, though vite-plugin-preload.ts unconditionally injects a /data/occurrences.parquet preload into every HTML file it transforms (and one per .wasm found in the bundle).

CAUSE: the plugin is registered in vite.config.ts, and the old eleventy-plugin-vite ran Vite rooted at .11ty-vite/ and never loaded that file — exactly as vite.config.ts's own closing comment says ('read by vitest and by production vite build/vite preview only'). So the LCP optimization it exists to provide has never shipped.

STATE AFTER beeatlas-d3y: still not running, now for a different reason — under backend integration no HTML reaches Vite at all, so transformIndexHtml cannot fire. The plugin is deliberately NOT registered in the new vite.config.ts, with a comment saying why. The file is still on disk.

TO REVIVE: emit the tags from Eleventy instead. The Vite manifest already names the hashed .wasm, and lib/vite-manifest.js already walks it — so this is a few lines in assetTags plus a decision about which pages should preload the parquet (the plugin injected it into every page, which is probably wrong for the 1668 content pages that never touch it).

Deliberately left out of beeatlas-d3y to keep that refactor behavior-preserving: turning a dormant optimization on mid-refactor would have made the before/after comparison unreadable.
acceptance_criteria: Either the preload tags are emitted from Eleventy on the pages that benefit, or vite-plugin-preload.ts is deleted with a note that the optimization was measured as not worth reviving.

title: Eliminate workbox-build: drop the redundant direct dep, then evaluate hand-rolling injectManifest
description:
Two parts, one cheap and certain, one an evaluation that may come back 'not worth it'.

PART 1 (certain). 'workbox-build' is declared as a direct runtime entry in package.json 'dependencies' but is never imported anywhere in the repo — the only occurrence in source is a comment at src/sw.ts:33. vite-plugin-pwa depends on it, so removing the direct declaration does NOT shrink the lockfile; the win is honesty about what the project actually depends on, plus it stops being a runtime dep for something that is build-only.

PART 2 (evaluate). The PWA build chain reaches 408 of the 811 packages in the lockfile — half the tree — with the workbox-build subtree accounting for 355 of them. eleventy.config.js:157,164 configures strategies: 'injectManifest', meaning src/sw.ts is hand-written and workbox-build's entire job is globbing _site and injecting a precache manifest into it. That is interface value rather than accumulated-bug-fix value, and is plausibly ~40 lines in scripts/postbuild-data.mjs.

EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE: the workbox RUNTIME packages imported by src/sw.ts — workbox-precaching, workbox-routing, workbox-strategies, workbox-expiration, workbox-cacheable-response, and workbox-window in src/sw-registration.ts. Those are 2-4 packages each and encode the offline-correctness edge cases fought through in Phase 151. They stay.
design:
Part 2 risk: the precache manifest is not just a file list — revision hashing, URL normalization, and the cleanupOutdatedCaches / precache-integrity contract with workbox-precaching all have to keep matching what workbox-precaching expects at runtime. src/tests/build-output.data.test.ts already asserts the emitted manifest is JSON-format with 'url' entries (around lines 356-363), which gives a starting oracle.

If the evaluation concludes the manifest contract is too fiddly to reimplement safely, close Part 2 with reason 'wontfix: injectManifest contract not worth reimplementing' and keep Part 1.
acceptance_criteria:
Part 1:
- 'workbox-build' removed from package.json dependencies
- Build, npm test, and the SW still work; lockfile total unchanged (~811) as expected

Part 2 (if pursued):
- vite-plugin-pwa removed; precache manifest generated in scripts/postbuild-data.mjs
- Lockfile drops by roughly 400 packages
- Offline cold-start still passes on real iOS per the Phase 151 checks — this is the gate, not unit tests

Both:
- Update src/tests/build-output.data.test.ts, which asserts package.json membership (OFF-02 ~line 412, D-13 ~line 427)
notes:
PART 1 SHIPPED in f3387eea. As predicted, the installed tree is unchanged (594 before and after) — vite-plugin-pwa still pulls workbox-build. package.json just stopped claiming a direct dependency the code never imported.

PART 2 RE-SCOPED 2026-07-30 — my '~40 lines in postbuild-data.mjs' estimate in the description above was WRONG, and the correction matters more than the original claim.

Reading eleventy.config.js:155-185 properly, vite-plugin-pwa is doing TWO jobs here, not one:
  (a) precache manifest generation — genuinely small in isolation, BUT the config semantics are not. globPatterns includes '.wasm' because the wa-sqlite binary must be precached or the SQL worker can't init offline and the Loading curtain hangs forever (Phase 151 real-device UAT, PWA-03). modifyURLPrefix exists to satisfy the precache cache-key contract. maximumFileSizeToCacheInBytes is D-03. Each line is a bug report someone already filed.
  (b) bundling the TypeScript service worker — 'filename: sw.ts' triggers a whole second Vite build producing _site/app/sw.js. Replacing this is not manifest work at all; it is standing up another build.

By the epic's own axis, (a)'s VALUE is accumulated bug fixes rather than a convenient interface — so it is a keep, not a rewrite. That is the opposite of what I wrote when filing this.

Measured for the record: workbox-build's 355-package subtree is 91 @babel/*, 32 rollup-related, 16 workbox/surma, 216 other. The Babel+Rollup half (~123) exists for the generateSW code path this project does not use — but an npm install cannot be subset, so it comes along regardless. title: Backfill elevation from a DEM for the four non-Ecdysis arms
description:
elevation_m is populated on only 45% of occurrences, and the gap is not random — it is an entire-arm gap. Every occurrence has coordinates; elevation could be derived from a DEM for nearly all of them.

COVERAGE TODAY (public/data/occurrences.db, 98,775 rows)
  specimen ............. 49,919 rows, 88.6% have elevation
  inat_expert .......... 28,850 rows,  0%
  checklist ............ 19,929 rows,  0%
  waba_specimen ........      40 rows,  0%
  provisional_sample ...      37 rows,  0%
Cause: elevation_m is read from Ecdysis minimum_elevation_in_meters (int_ecdysis_base.sql:25); int_combined.sql hardcodes NULL::INTEGER for the other four arms (lines 115, 167, 255, 319).

SIZE OF THE WORK
34,628 non-checklist rows have coordinates but no elevation, resolving to only 27,580 distinct coordinates. This is a cacheable one-time lookup keyed by rounded coordinate, not a per-row API call — and the nightly delta is small. Backfill would take the iNat arm from 0% to ~100% and overall coverage from 45% to ~89%.

TWO CONSTRAINTS, BOTH FALLING OUT OF THE GEOGRAPHY-FILTER GRILLING
1. DO NOT BACKFILL CHECKLIST ROWS. 31% of them (6,090 of 19,929) sit on 45 shared placeholder points — 683 King County rows are parked on a single coordinate in downtown Seattle. A DEM lookup there returns the elevation of that placeholder, not of anywhere a bee was found. It would be fabricated data wearing the same column name as measured data.
2. KEEP DERIVED ELEVATION DISTINGUISHABLE FROM RECORDED ELEVATION. A separate column (e.g. elevation_dem_m) plus provenance, not a silent COALESCE into elevation_m. A DEM sample at a coordinate whose positional accuracy is up to 100 m (the expert feed's acc_below_or_unknown=100) is uncertain in steep terrain in a way a collector's recorded elevation is not. This also keeps the artifacts.toml derived-vs-authoritative discipline intact: recorded elevation is upstream data, DEM elevation is derived and rebuildable.

SOURCE — NOT YET CHOSEN
USGS 3DEP (10 m, public domain) is the obvious candidate for Washington. Prefer a local raster sampled offline over a network elevation API: the pipeline is an offline nightly with no runtime service dependency, and 27,580 points is a trivial raster sample but a meaningful API bill and failure surface. Confirm the licence permits redistribution of derived values before shipping.

WHY IT MATTERS
Unblocks the honest version of "all the species of Bombus above 1700m". Under the geography-filter bead's D-02 (elevation demands positive evidence), any taxon with no elevation-bearing record is simply absent from the answer — so today that question is answered from the Ecdysis arm alone, silently ignoring 28,850 community observations.
design:
STELIS GRAPH (missing from the original write-up).

1. ORDERING IS THE WHOLE RISK. This backfill produces data that dbt reads (int_combined must project it alongside the Ecdysis elevation_m). So it needs a declared edge placing it BEFORE dbt-build, expressed the Stelis way: an artifact it #:outputs that dbt-build lists in #:inputs. Do not rely on declaration order in the task list — the graph, not the file, is the schedule.

This is the same class of hazard as the pipeline-ordering memory (cross-repo beeatlas<->stelis): the checklist step mutates ecdysis_data.occurrences.canonical_name in place while the ecdysis loader writes with write_disposition='replace', so an ecdysis_data->checklist edge is what keeps canonical_name from being NULL at dbt time. run.py's linear STEPS used to enforce that implicitly; under Stelis it is an explicit edge or it is nothing. Any new writer in this neighbourhood inherits the same obligation.

2. DO NOT PUT THE DEM RASTER IN THE GRAPH AS AN INPUT. Stelis is content-addressed; a multi-GB 3DEP raster as a task input means hashing it every run. Prefer a small derived coordinate->elevation lookup (keyed by rounded coordinate, ~27,580 entries) as the graph artifact, with the raster sampled out-of-band and the lookup treated as the cacheable unit. Incremental runs then only sample coordinates not already in the lookup.

3. PROVENANCE. Recorded elevation is upstream/authoritative; DEM elevation is derived and rebuildable. Under artifacts.toml's two regimes (docs/adr/0002) that is a 'derived' artifact — which also means it may be a dbt model and IS subject to baseline_diff, unlike the authoritative loaders.
acceptance_criteria: Non-checklist occurrences with coordinates carry a DEM-derived elevation; overall elevation coverage rises from 45% to ~89%; checklist rows are NOT backfilled and the reason is documented at the code; derived elevation is a distinct column from recorded elevation with provenance, never a silent COALESCE; the lookup is keyed by distinct coordinate (~27,580) rather than per row; DEM source licence permits redistribution of derived values; pytest covers the backfill and the checklist exclusion.
close_reason: Shipped: elevation_dem_m from USGS 3DEP 1 arcsec. Non-checklist coverage 0%->100% (overall 44.8%->79.8%); checklist deliberately 0% and asserted. Separate column, no COALESCE. ADR 0015. beeatlas d044677f + stelis 79207b1.

title: Intermittent flake: api test_verify_cookie_rejects_tampered_token fails ~1-in-15 full-suite runs
description: api/tests/test_session.py::test_verify_cookie_rejects_tampered_token fails intermittently in the full 'cd data && uv run pytest' run, but passes in isolation and passed 8/8 consecutive full runs afterward. Observed twice on 2026-07-18 while validating the st-kse commit. Not caused by that change (it touches data/tests only; the failing test is in api/). Suspected order-dependence via pytest-randomly or a time/timestamp boundary in the signed-cookie verification (session.py mints a timestamped token). Reproduce by looping the full suite; a --randomly-seed did not reproduce reliably, which argues against pure order-dependence.
close_reason: Not a flake in api/session.py — a latent bug in the test's tampering logic. It mutated the token's LAST character, which encodes the tail of the base64url'd HMAC: 20 signature bytes (160 bits) span 27 chars (162 bits), and the decoder ignores the 2 slack bits, so {Y,Z,a,b} all decode identically. The encoder only ever emits the canonical member (Y) of that class, so whenever the signature ended in Y, swapping in 'a' produced a different string with an identical decoded signature — verification succeeded and the assert failed. Rate = 1/16 reachable final chars; measured 1291/20000 (6.45%, 1-in-15.5) across varied timestamps, matching the reported ~1-in-15. No order dependence (hence the unreproducible --randomly-seed) and no timestamp boundary; the only per-run variable is the embedded timestamp changing the HMAC. Fix: mutate token[0], which always carries 6 significant bits. Verified 0/50000 accepted post-fix, plus 24/24 clean full-suite runs.

title: refresh-geo.sh fast-path deploy no longer reaches the frontend (dead unhashed paths) — retire or rewrite
description:
Found while closing beeatlas-3q8. data/refresh-geo.sh uploads counties/ecoregions geojson to the UNHASHED stable keys s3://.../data/counties.geojson etc. and invalidates those paths. But since the content-hash+manifest migration, the frontend's resolveDataUrl (src/manifest.ts) resolves ONLY hashed names from manifest.json — it never reads the bare keys, and refresh-geo.sh does NOT update manifest.json. So the 'fast geo redeploy' writes to paths nothing reads and its changes never reach the live site. The hyq fix made it upload the CLEANED content (was raw), but that didn't address the deeper deadness.

DECISION NEEDED (user):
(a) Retire refresh-geo.sh — the full nightly is the only real publish path; a geo-only change just waits for the next nightly (or a manual nightly run). Simplest.
(b) Rewrite it to do a proper hashed publish for the two geo artifacts: hash counties.clean.geojson/ecoregions.clean.geojson, upload hashed names, MERGE the two keys into the live manifest.json (pull, patch, push), invalidate /data/manifest.json. More faithful to 'fast path' but must not clobber other manifest keys written by a concurrent nightly.

Also: stale relic objects at the bare keys (occurrences.parquet, species.json, seasonality.json, counties.geojson, ecoregions.geojson — last modified 2026-05-16) sit on S3 served at 200 but read by nothing now that fetch-data.sh was repointed. Consider S3 cleanup as part of whichever option (needs explicit go-ahead; destructive).
close_reason: Retired: deleted data/refresh-geo.sh (only self-reference; no docs/CI/run.py deps). Geo changes now ride the nightly's hashed-publish path. Also deleted the 5 stale bare S3 relics (counties/ecoregions.geojson, occurrences.parquet, seasonality.json, species.json, all frozen 2026-05-16) — verified 200->403.

title: infra/: migrate off ts-node@10 to enable TypeScript 7
description:
infra/ (CDK) is pinned to TypeScript ~6.0.3 because its CDK runner ts-node@10.9.2 is incompatible with the TS7 native (Go) compiler: ts-node calls a TS host API the native package doesn't expose (fails in readConfig with 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading fileExists)'). ts-node@10.9.2 is unmaintained and will not gain native-TS support. The infra test runs in NO CI workflow so this went unnoticed. Worth fixing in the same pass (align @types/node with the TS version, or bump infra TS). They annotate, never block — distinct from the integrity gate (which is an operator alarm that stops the nightly publish) and from a correction (which changes a published value). See stelis ADR 0006 for that split and ADR 0009 for the third modality.

VENUE IS SETTLED: these live in dbt, not in Stelis. stelis ADR 0008 decision 1 held the design pass ADR 0006 asked for and settled the dbt-vs-Stelis-Datalog fork toward dbt — dup collector-day, out-of-state and bee-vs-flower are per-record or per-cluster LEAF predicates (a group-by-count, a spatial predicate, a classification). None propagate recursively, so none are more natural in Datalog than in SQL, and they earn no substrate. Do not reopen that question; ordinary marts columns published through dbt-build, no Stelis-side change at all.

FILED P4 DELIBERATELY. Nothing mechanical blocks this — no missing capability, no dependency. What is missing is a definition per rule and a reader who wants the answer. Carried over from stelis st-8v3, which was closed 2026-08-04 as superseded by the ADR 0008 verdict; this holds the half that survived.
design:
FOUR THINGS ARE UNRESOLVED, and the first three are per-rule judgment calls that must be made before any SQL.

1. THE RULES ARE NAMES, NOT PREDICATES.
   - dup collector-day: same collector + same day + same species? same place too? Several genuine specimens in one day are normal, so the rule must say what makes a set SUSPECT rather than merely repeated.
   - out-of-state: needs a boundary rule and a decision about edge records. May not be a flag at all — a record outside the atlas scope might be an EXCLUSION, which is a different modality.
   - bee-vs-flower: which direction, and note it PARTLY EXISTS already. collectors_events_export.py resolves unresolved non-bee bycatch to species_slug=None with an iNat fallback; nothing equivalent lives in the marts. So this is relocating export-time logic into dbt — a refactor with a compatibility question, not a greenfield rule.

2. NO RENDER SURFACE IS DECIDED. Flags are published derived data, but the collector event feed is the only surface that shows INDIVIDUAL records; species pages and maps are aggregates where a per-record flag has nowhere to go. Until someone says where a flag appears and what a reader does about it, the column is write-only.

3. THE TRIAGE POSTDATES THE ORIGINAL FRAMING. stelis ADR 0009 made corrections a real third modality after these three were nominated. Run flag / gate / correction per rule: this-record-is-wrong may want a correction (change the value, cite what was overruled) rather than a flag (publish it with a note). One of the three may turn out not to be a flag.

4. NO PULLING QUESTION YET. These were nominated in the Horizon 1 data-quality push and survived two ADR passes as a leftover, not as an answer to a question anyone has. What makes this ready is someone looking at a collector page and wanting the dubious records marked — not a decision that can be made in the abstract.
acceptance_criteria: Per rule taken on: (a) the predicate is written down before the SQL, with the suspect-vs-merely-repeated line drawn explicitly; (b) it has been triaged as flag vs gate vs correction and the choice recorded; (c) a named surface renders it, so it is not a write-only column; (d) flagged records still COUNT — a flag must not change record counts, or it will move the integrity gate. Partial delivery is fine: one well-defined rule with a reader beats three columns nobody sees.
